insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Mediclaim Policy (sum insured Rs 3,00,000 + Rs 20,000 cumulative bonus)
facts: The complainant's wife was admitted to a Mumbai hospital in February 2020 with sepsis, cellulitis and uncontrolled diabetes, spent part of the stay in the ICU and died during the admission. The claim of Rs 2,77,712 was short-settled: the insurer disallowed ICU/room rent above eligibility and also reduced consultation, investigation and physiotherapy charges proportionately. The complainant accepted the room-rent and non-medical deductions but disputed the proportionate cuts (Rs 21,000 sought), producing the hospital tariff which showed that consultation, investigation and lab charges did not vary with room or ICU category.
insurer_reason: ICU charges of Rs 8,750/day exceeded the ICU limit of 2% of sum insured per day, so all other hospital expenses except medicines were paid in the same proportion under clause 3.2 (proportionate deduction); remaining deductions were non-medical items under Annexure 2.
reasoning: The Forum accepted the hospital tariff showing that all charges other than the bed charge were the same whether the patient was in a ward or the ICU. Disallowing room rent above the limit and non-medical items was in order, but reducing other charges proportionately when the hospital has no class-based tariff was held unjustified and against IRDAI guidelines; the insurer itself conceded that proportionate deduction would not apply to doctor fees and investigations at this hospital. The balance admissible expenses deducted proportionately were ordered to be paid (amount not quantified in the award).
rules_or_clauses_cited: New India Mediclaim Policy clause 3.1(b) - ICU/ICCU expenses up to 2% of sum insured per day
Clause 3.2 - proportionate deduction (all other expenses except medicines)
Annexure 2 - non-medical items
IRDAI guidelines on proportionate deduction (as referred to by the Forum)
key_quote: reducing other charges in proportion to the entitled room category in the absence of a class-based tariff is not justified and is against IRDAI guidelines in this regard
source_pages: PDF pages 605-609 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Floater Mediclaim Policy (sum insured Rs 3,00,000)
facts: The insured was hospitalised in Mumbai for 7 days in April 2020 for acute febrile illness with chronic kidney disease and hypertension; cashless was not given. The reimbursement claim of Rs 1,31,600 was settled for Rs 57,335. The insured had occupied a room of Rs 4,500/day against an eligibility of Rs 3,000/day. The complainant disputed the deductions (Rs 74,265), mainly PPE kit and swab test charges, and later submitted additional swab test bills.
insurer_reason: Excess room and nursing charges disallowed (eligible Rs 3,000/day); doctor fees and hospital service charges paid in proportion to the eligible room rent under policy condition 3.1; diet charges not payable; PPE kits paid for only one day for a non-Covid patient; investigation charges lacked a break-up. On reassessment the TPA found a further Rs 6,538 payable.
reasoning: The Forum held that deducting diet charges, excess room charges and the proportionate reduction of other charges were as per policy terms and in order. However, disallowing PPE kit charges during Covid times was not justified even for a non-Covid patient, and the additional investigation bills had to be considered. The insurer was directed to pay the PPE deduction, the admissible investigation charges and the Rs 6,538 it had already found payable.
rules_or_clauses_cited: New India Floater Mediclaim policy condition 3.1 - room rent limit and proportionate deduction
Non-payable diet charges
key_quote: the disallowance of PPE Kit charges during Covid times even though the complainant was a non-covid patient, is not justified

forum: State Commission Karnataka (Karnataka State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Bengaluru)
case_ref: Appeal No. 1411/2019 (arising from Complaint No. 51/2018, District Forum Chikmagalur) - V. Rama Rao v. New India Assurance
insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Mediclaim policy held since 1978, renewed as New India Mediclaim 2012 policy (sum insured Rs 3,00,000)
facts: The complainant, aged about 80, had held a mediclaim policy with the insurer since 1978, later renewed on Mediclaim 2012 terms. In June 2017 he underwent prostate and hernia surgery at a Bengaluru hospital costing Rs 3,58,384, but the TPA paid only Rs 1,23,971. The deductions included non-payable medicines and consumables, a pro-rata (proportionate) deduction of Rs 1,14,761, the hospital discount and tax, and the Mediclaim 2012 clause paying only 80% of admissible claims for insureds over 55 without 48 months of claim-free cover. The District Forum dismissed his complaint, holding he had admitted reading the new policy terms.
insurer_reason: Claim settled as per Mediclaim 2012 terms: room rent restricted to 1% of sum insured per day with proportionate deduction of other charges, consumables non-payable, and only 80% of the admissible claim payable for an insured over 55 years without 48 months of claim-free continuous cover.
reasoning: Relying on the Supreme Court's decision in Jacob Punnen v. United India Insurance (2021), the Commission held that the insurer had not notified this long-standing policyholder of the revised, more restrictive terms before renewal, so settling the claim on those terms was deficient. It also relied on the NCDRC ruling in New India Assurance v. A.K. Kariappa that applying a mechanical proportionate deduction, instead of finding out what the hospital would have charged for the eligible room category, is a faulty procedure. The insurer was directed to pay up to the Rs 3,00,000 sum insured less the amount paid (Rs 1,76,029) with 6% interest, Rs 25,000 compensation and Rs 10,000 costs.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Mediclaim 2012 clause 3.2 - 80% of admissible claim for insured over 55 without 48 months claim-free cover
Room rent limit 1% of sum insured per day with proportionate deduction
Jacob Punnen v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. (Supreme Court, 09.12.2021)
New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. A.K. Kariappa (NCDRC, Revision Petition No. 766/2011)
key_quote: The procedure adopted by the insurance company was faulty.
notes: Quoted by the State Commission from the NCDRC order in New India Assurance v. A.K. Kariappa.

forum: State Commission Gujarat (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Gujarat State, Ahmedabad)
case_ref: First Appeal No. 897/2022 (arising from Complaint No. 580/2019, District Commission Surat) - The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Vijiyan Ponnu Nadar
insurer_name: The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Mediclaim policy, silver plan (sum insured Rs 3,00,000)
facts: The complainant was hospitalised in Surat for three days in October 2018 after slipping from a scooter. The insurer paid Rs 1,30,126 cashless and deducted Rs 92,363 under various heads, including proportionate deductions on surgeon fees, duty doctor, lab, X-ray, gases and physiotherapy, OT consumables and procedure charges treated as included in OT, non-medical items, nursing charges and a 10% co-payment on implants. The District Commission awarded the full Rs 92,363 and the insurer appealed.
insurer_reason: Room rent eligibility was 1% of sum insured (Rs 3,000/day) and a higher room was taken, so proportionate deduction applied; the silver plan carries a 10% co-payment; nursing and non-medical items not payable; OT consumables and procedure charges included in OT charges.
reasoning: The State Commission found that the policy wording justified only four deductions: excess room rent (Rs 3,000), nursing charges (Rs 1,050), non-medical items (Rs 6,456) and the 10% co-payment on implants (Rs 16,065), totalling Rs 26,571. The insurer could not justify the proportionate cuts on surgeon/doctor fees, investigations, gases and physiotherapy or the 'included in OT' deductions (Rs 65,792), which amounted to deficiency in service. The District Commission's award was reduced from Rs 92,363 to Rs 65,792.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Policy clause 1.1/1.2 - room rent 1% of sum insured per day and nursing charges
Clause 3.8 - co-payment definition (10% silver plan)
Clause 4.17 - non-medical expenses
Industrial Promotion & Investment Corporation of Orissa v. New India Assurance (2016) 15 SCC 315 - cited by insurer
key_quote: the appellant has shown deficiency in service

forum: State Commission West Bengal (West Bengal State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kolkata)
case_ref: First Appeal No. A/465/2018 (arising from CC/124/2017, District Forum North 24 Parganas) - Santi Ranjan Banik v. The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Mediclaim Policy (sum insured not stated in order)
facts: The complainant, insured under a New India mediclaim policy, was admitted to a higher category of room than his entitlement. The insurer reimbursed room rent at the admissible rate and paid consultation, laboratory/diagnostic and other expenses, except medicines, in proportion. The District Forum rejected his complaint of short reimbursement, and he appealed arguing that consultation and diagnostic charges should have been paid in full under the policy clauses.
insurer_reason: Clause 3.1(d): room rent, boarding and nursing limited to 1% of sum insured per day (2% for ICU/ICCU); if the room rate exceeds the limit, all other hospital expenses except medicines are paid in the same proportion as the admissible rate bears to the actual room rate.
reasoning: Reading clause 3.1(d), the Commission held that once a patient is admitted to a room/ICU above the entitled category, all admissible expenses other than medicines are reimbursable at proportionate rates and not at actuals. It found no inaccuracy in the TPA's deductions and held that the complainant had misread the policy, so no relief was granted.
rules_or_clauses_cited: New India Mediclaim Policy clause 3.1(d) - room rent cap and proportionate reimbursement (medicines excepted)
key_quote: all other admissible expenses is reimbursable at proportionate rates and not on actual

forum: State Commission West Bengal (West Bengal State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kolkata)
case_ref: First Appeal No. A/98/2017 (arising from CC/508/2013, District Forum Kolkata-I (North)) - Niraj Kajaria v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
insurer_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: United India mediclaim policy (sum insured Rs 4,25,000)
facts: The complainant claimed Rs 2,41,204 for his wife's hospitalisation in September 2012: a hospital bill of Rs 95,842 plus Rs 1,45,362 towards doctor fees paid separately by cheque, implant, medicines and pathology. The insurer paid Rs 1,29,056. The wife stayed five days in rooms charged at Rs 9,000 and Rs 5,400 per day against an entitlement of Rs 4,250 per day. The District Forum dismissed the complaint.
insurer_reason: The patient occupied rooms above her entitlement, so room rent was capped and doctor, nursing and other expenses were reimbursed proportionately; doctor fees paid directly outside the hospital bill were not reimbursed.
reasoning: The Commission upheld the room-rent deduction of Rs 12,950 as fully justified by the 1%-of-sum-insured cap (Rs 4,250 x 5 days). But it found the proportionate deductions were wrongly computed - for example, on a day when the room was 21.29% above eligibility, 52.77% of the OT equipment charge was deducted - and held that doctor fees paid directly could not be refused without written reasons, given the insurer's own head-office guideline. The insurer was ordered to recompute, pay the balance with 9% interest, furnish a calculation sheet and pay Rs 25,000 litigation costs.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Room rent entitlement 1% of sum insured per day
Proportionate reimbursement of other expenses for higher room category
Insurer's head-office guideline on reimbursement of doctor fees paid by cheque
key_quote: the Respondents did not act bona fide while figuring out the admissible amount

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India New Mediclaim 2012 Policy (sum insured Rs 10,00,000)
facts: The complainant underwent arthroscopic ACL reconstruction of the left knee at a Mumbai sports-medicine hospital in November-December 2019 and claimed Rs 2,85,691. The TPA initially deducted Rs 65,332 and later paid part of it after clarifications from the hospital. The remaining dispute was Rs 10,890 billed separately by the hospital for anaesthesia machine and gases; the treating doctor certified that these charges are patient-specific and not included in OT charges.
insurer_reason: Anaesthesia machine and gases are consumables forming part of OT charges under the standard definition of OT and should not be billed separately; OT and anaesthesia charges in the bill had already been paid. (Separately, Rs 17,947 of items such as caps, gauze, masks, gloves and food were deducted as non-payable.)
reasoning: The Forum noted that the hospital had billed the anaesthesia equipment and gases separately and clarified they were not part of OT charges; had they been included in OT charges the insurer would have paid them. Disallowing them merely because of how the hospital structured its bill was not justified, so the further Rs 10,890 was ordered to be paid.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Standard definition of operation theatre (OT) charges
IRDAI list of non-payable items (items such as caps, masks, gloves, gauze)
key_quote: since the hospital has not included these charges in the O.T. charges and has billed for it separately, disallowance of the same is not justified and cannot be sustained
source_pages: PDF pages 351-354 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Mediclaim Policy (sum insured Rs 2,00,000 + Rs 50,000 cumulative bonus)
facts: The complainant was admitted to a Mumbai hospital in December 2020 with a diabetic wound of the right leg and underwent split-skin grafting of the right foot with vacuum-assisted closure (VAC). Against a final bill of Rs 1,07,508, Rs 77,641 was settled cashless. He disputed the deductions, in particular Rs 7,392 for a drainage kit, which he said was not a dressing item.
insurer_reason: Rs 2,700 of nursing/RMO charges are included in room charges; Rs 23,837 was deducted as non-medical expenses, including Rs 7,392 for the drainage kit, which is not payable under clause 4.4.17 and Annexure II (item 180 - 'any kit not specified').
reasoning: The Forum held that the drainage kit is a non-medical item listed as not payable in Annexure II (item 180) of the policy, so the settlement was in order and no relief could be granted.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Clause 4.4.17 - non-medical items excluded
Annexure II item 180 - any kit not specified
key_quote: Drainage Kit which is not payable as per Annexure II (Item No.180)

forum: State Commission Delhi (Delhi State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission)
case_ref: First Appeal No. 1270/2013 (arising from Complaint No. 1249 of 2010, District Forum, I.P. Estate, New Delhi) - National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Amit Mittal
insurer_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: National Insurance mediclaim policy (2009-10)
facts: The complainant was hospitalised in Gurgaon in November 2009 after a fall injured his left knee. He claimed Rs 88,067, which included a knee support, equipment charges, small items such as micropore and bandages, and physiotherapy/doctor visits at home, but the TPA approved only Rs 9,527. The District Forum awarded the full claim with 9% interest and Rs 35,000, and the insurer appealed.
insurer_reason: Deductions under exclusion 4.16 (external/durable medical equipment usable at home, e.g., knee support), 4.17 (non-medical items) and 4.26 (doctor's home visits and nursing/physiotherapy at home during pre- and post-hospitalisation), totalling Rs 78,490.
reasoning: Applying the principle that insurance contracts are construed strictly (Sushilaben Indravadan Gandhi v. New India Assurance, SC 2020), the State Commission held the deducted items fell within the exclusion clauses. It set aside the District Forum's order and directed payment of only the originally approved Rs 9,527 (with 9% interest if not paid by 31.03.2021).
rules_or_clauses_cited: Exclusion 4.16 - external/durable medical and non-medical equipment
Exclusion 4.17 - non-medical expenses
Exclusion 4.26 - doctor's home visit / attendant / nursing during pre- and post-hospitalisation
Sushilaben Indravadan Gandhi v. New India Assurance (2020 SCC OnLine SC 367)
key_quote: the Insurance Company is permitted to make deduction of the aforesaid expenses from the insurance claim as per the exclusionary clauses in the insurance policy

insurer_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: National Mediclaim Policy (sum insured Rs 3,00,000 + Rs 1,40,000)
facts: The complainant's wife had right-eye cataract surgery at a Mumbai eye clinic in November 2019. The claim of Rs 52,935 was settled for Rs 34,000, citing the 'customary and reasonable' clause. The policy had no specific cap for cataract surgery, and the complainant argued that bigger hospitals would have charged more.
insurer_reason: Reasonable and customary charges (clause 3.29): comparable Mumbai hospitals charged Rs 18,000-30,000 for cataract surgery; package rates are negotiated with network (PPN) hospitals; for non-PPN reimbursement claims only the cost of a monofocal lens is payable; the insured should act as if uninsured when agreeing to rates.
reasoning: The Forum held that PPN rates are negotiated between the insurer/TPA and specific hospitals and cannot be used as the benchmark for a non-network hospital. The policy did not require treatment at a PPN hospital, had no cap on cataract surgery and did not restrict cover to a monofocal lens, and the expenses were not unreasonable. The balance of Rs 18,935 was ordered to be paid, less non-medical expenses if any.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Clause 3.29 - reasonable and customary charges
Preferred Provider Network (PPN) package rates
key_quote: it would not be proper to compare the rates charged by non-PPN hospitals with that of PPN hospitals
source_pages: PDF pages 388-391 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Mediclaim Policy (sum insured Rs 3,00,000)
facts: The complainant's son, continuously insured since 2001, had surgery in Mumbai in August-September 2020 for a comminuted fracture of the upper right humerus after an accident. The claim of Rs 3,09,351 was settled for Rs 1,67,379. Deductions included Rs 81,500 out of a Rs 1,25,000 surgeon's fee under the reasonable & customary clause, excess room rent (Rs 3,500/day vs Rs 3,000 eligible) with proportionate deductions, C-arm, dressing, OT replacement medicines and non-medical items. It was the first claim in about 19 years of cover.
insurer_reason: Surgeon's fee restricted under the Reasonable & Customary clause 2.37; excess room rent and proportionate deduction under clause 3.2; C-arm charges included in OT; dressing included in nursing; OT replacement medicines without break-up; non-medical items not payable.
reasoning: The Forum upheld the room-rent cap and proportionate deduction under clause 3.2 (which exempts only medicines) and the non-medical deductions. It allowed C-arm (Rs 16,000), dressing (Rs 3,500) and OT replacement (Rs 10,900) as genuinely billed. On the surgeon's fee, it held the insurer may apply the reasonable & customary clause by comparing prevailing charges in the area even without a specific cap, but to strike a balance allowed half (Rs 40,750) of the Rs 81,500 deducted.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Clause 2.37 - reasonable and customary charges
Clause 3.2 - room rent 1% of sum insured and proportionate deduction (except medicines)
key_quote: even in the absence of a specific capping in the policy, the Company is within its right to limit the expenses payable for a particular procedure by comparing the charges prevalent in the same geographical area

insurer_name: Manipal Cigna Health Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: ProHealth Protect family floater (sum insured Rs 5,50,000)
facts: The complainant's wife was hospitalised for Covid-19 from 8 to 13 October 2020. The hospital bill was Rs 1,56,193, but the reimbursement claim was settled for only Rs 36,592. The complainant pointed out that a relative treated for Covid in the same hospital at the same time was reimbursed by another insurer with only a co-payment deduction.
insurer_reason: Covid-19 has no established protocol or standardised costs, so the claim was settled at the General Insurance Council's schedule of Covid treatment rates: Rs 59,550 deducted as in excess of GIC rates, plus Rs 3,098 for non-medical items (masks, caps, sheets) and Rs 300 miscellaneous charges.
reasoning: The Forum observed that the GI Council tariff was never circulated to policyholders or disclosed at claim intimation, had not been reviewed as expected and did not match actual hospital charges. As per IRDAI guidelines Covid claims must be assessed under each policy's terms; this policy had no head-wise ceilings and the insurer raised no specific objection on the reasonableness of the bill. Only the non-payable items (Rs 3,098) and miscellaneous charges (Rs 300) were upheld and the balance Rs 1,16,203 was awarded.
rules_or_clauses_cited: General Insurance Council schedule of rates for Covid-19 treatment (held not binding for reimbursement under this policy)
IRDAI guidelines that Covid claims be assessed as per the respective policy terms
key_quote: The tariff given by GI council is not circulated amongst the policy holders nor was the complainant made aware of it at the time of claim intimation.
source_pages: PDF pages 728-730 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

forum: State Commission Gujarat (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Gujarat State, Ahmedabad)
case_ref: First Appeal No. 690/2017 (arising from Complaint No. 426/2016, District Commission Vadodara) - Dr. Rikesh T. Majmudar v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
insurer_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: United India mediclaim policy (sum insured Rs 5,00,000)
facts: The complainant, a surgeon, underwent cataract surgery on both eyes in February-March 2016 with foldable multifocal intraocular lenses, spending Rs 70,000 per eye (Rs 1,40,000 in total). The insurer paid Rs 29,000 per eye, allowing only Rs 10,000 per lens (the price of a unifocal lens) against Rs 51,000 billed for each multifocal lens. The District Commission awarded only Rs 20,000 of the Rs 82,000 deducted, and the complainant appealed.
insurer_reason: A multifocal lens primarily has a cosmetic benefit of eliminating spectacles; cost of spectacles, surgery for correction of vision and cosmetic treatment are excluded (clauses 4.6(b), 4.7), and only medically necessary, reasonable and customary expenses are payable (clauses 3.22, 3.33).
reasoning: The Commission held the procedure was a cataract surgery, not a cosmetic one, and the insurer produced no contrary evidence; the spectacles/contact lens exclusion concerns external aids, not an implanted lens. The policy set no limit on cataract charges or type of lens, so the insurer could not override the treating doctor's choice of implant or use the reasonable & customary clause to restrict it. The full Rs 82,000 was awarded with 8% interest from the date of complaint.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Clause 3.22 - medical expenses
Clause 3.33 - reasonable and customary charges
Exclusion 4.6(b) - cosmetic treatment / correction of eyesight
Exclusion 4.7 - cost of spectacles, contact lenses and hearing aids
Narendra D. Jobanputra v. Oriental Insurance (Gujarat State Commission, Appeal No. 1378/2014)
key_quote: Selection of type of implants cannot be decided by insurer.

insurer_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Individual Health Insurance Policy - Gold (sum insured Rs 5,50,000)
facts: The complainant had right-eye cataract surgery at a Mumbai eye institute in January 2020 under a policy running from 18 April 2019. The claim of Rs 1,44,338 was settled for Rs 40,000, with surgeon, procedure and implant charges deducted as higher than reasonable and customary. The complainant relied on the policy condition limiting cataract claims to actual expenses or 25% of the sum insured, whichever is less.
insurer_reason: Charges exceeded reasonable and customary rates (clause 3.33); the insurer also said the Gold policy capped cataract surgery at Rs 40,000 per eye under revised terms introduced from 25.03.2019, with all renewals after 25.06.2019 issued on the new terms.
reasoning: The Forum found that the complainant's policy was issued before the revised terms became compulsory and he had not opted for them, so condition 1.2.1 (actual expenses or 25% of sum insured, whichever is less) applied. Where the policy itself fixes the cataract limit, deducting under the reasonable & customary clause was not justified; the entitlement was Rs 1,37,500 (25% of Rs 5,50,000), so a further Rs 97,500 was payable.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Condition 1.2.1 - cataract limit: actual expenses or 25% of sum insured, whichever is less
Clause 3.33 - reasonable and customary charges
Revised Gold policy terms with Rs 40,000 per-eye cataract cap (effective 25.03.2019 / compulsory for renewals after 25.06.2019)
key_quote: the deduction of claim amount on the ground of Reasonable and Customary Clause of the policy is not justified, the claim has to be paid as per policy terms and conditions

forum: Supreme Court of India (civil appeal from NCDRC)
case_ref: Civil Appeal No. 6778 of 2013 - Jacob Punnen & Anr. v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
insurer_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: United India mediclaim policy renewed annually since 1982 (cover Rs 8,00,000 for two insureds in 2008-09)
facts: The appellants had held a mediclaim policy with the insurer since 1982 and renewed it for March 2008-March 2009 on the insurer's renewal reminder. In June 2008 one of them underwent angioplasty and claimed Rs 3,82,705, but the insurer paid Rs 2,00,000, relying on a new term in the renewed policy capping such procedures at 70% of the policy limit subject to Rs 2,00,000 per surgery. The District Forum ordered a further Rs 1,75,000, but the State Commission and NCDRC held that the renewed policy was a fresh contract binding on the insured.
insurer_reason: Policy terms had changed on renewal; the 2008-09 policy capped procedures such as angioplasty at 70% of the policy limit subject to an overall limit of Rs 2,00,000 per surgery, and the insured had accepted the policy document.
reasoning: The Supreme Court held that an insurer is under a duty to inform existing policyholders, at renewal, of new limitations it is imposing so that they can choose suitable cover - an obligation now also reflected in the IRDA (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016. Accepting the renewal premium while keeping the insured unaware of the new cap was deficiency in service. The NCDRC and State Commission orders were set aside, the District Forum's award (Rs 1,75,000 plus Rs 5,000 compensation) was restored and the insurer was made to pay additional costs of Rs 50,000.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Consumer Protection Act, 1986 - deficiency in service
IRDA (Health Insurance) Regulations, 2016 - disclosure of changes on renewal (as discussed by the Court)
Biman Krishna Bose v. United India Insurance (2001) 6 SCC 477
key_quote: Its failure to inform the policy holders resulted in deficiency of service.

forum: Insurance Ombudsman (centre not named in the published 2017-18 mediclaim award compilation)
case_ref: Case No. 18 in the Individual Mediclaim award compilation - complainant v. Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd. (award dated 01.11.2017)
insurer_name: The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Oriental mediclaim policy (sum insured Rs 1,00,000); patient also covered under an employer policy with United India (sum insured Rs 3,00,000)
facts: The complainant's mother was insured under an Oriental Insurance mediclaim policy and also under a policy taken through the complainant's employer with United India Insurance. She was hospitalised in Bareilly in May 2016 for coronary artery disease with diabetes and hypertension. United India settled the claim after deducting Rs 70,160 as 30% co-payment, and the balance claimed from Oriental was rejected.
insurer_reason: The co-payment portion deducted by one insurer cannot be claimed from another insurer.
reasoning: The complainant showed that the Oriental policy had no co-payment clause and no condition barring recovery of a co-payment deducted under another insurer's policy; by the policy's own definition, co-payment is a cost-sharing percentage that does not reduce the sum insured. The Ombudsman held the deduction on account of co-payment unjustified and directed the insurer to pay the co-payment amount to the insured.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Policy clause 2.8 - definition of co-payment (does not reduce sum insured)
Contribution between multiple health policies
key_quote: It was observed that deduction on account of co payment is unjustified.

insurer_name: The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Happy Family Floater Policy (sum insured Rs 5,00,000)
facts: The complainant, insured for more than 20 years, was hospitalised in Mumbai for Covid-19 in August 2020. His claim of Rs 1,60,952 was settled for Rs 71,643, and the deductions of Rs 89,309 were not explained to him. At the Forum's direction the insurer produced a break-up - excess room rent, proportionate doctor fees, investigations, PPE kits, miscellaneous charges, pre/post-hospitalisation items and a 10% co-payment of Rs 11,809 - and on review found a further Rs 34,638 payable.
insurer_reason: Deductions made on the basis of the government notification for Covid claims, proportionate deduction for a higher room, non-payable items and the 10% co-payment applicable under the policy.
reasoning: After analysing the break-up, the Forum allowed PPE kit charges of Rs 13,565 over and above the Rs 34,638 already conceded by the insurer and held all other deductions, including the 10% co-payment, to be in order. The insurer was directed to pay Rs 48,203 in full and final settlement, subject to availability of sum insured.
rules_or_clauses_cited: 10% co-payment under the policy
Proportionate deduction for higher room category
Government notification on Covid treatment charges (relied on by insurer)
key_quote: the Forum is of the view to allow PPE Kit Charges of Rs.13565/- deducted over and above Rs.34638/-

insurer_name: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Star Comprehensive Insurance Policy - 2015 (sum insured Rs 5,00,000 floater), ported
facts: The complainant had been continuously covered under mediclaim policies with a public sector insurer since 2000 and ported to the respondent insurer in August 2019 after his bank-linked product was discontinued. In the first month of the new policy he was hospitalised in Mumbai for acute internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The claim of Rs 43,061 was repudiated and his cover deleted because past bypass surgery (2013), facio-brachial paralysis, diabetes and hypertension were not disclosed in the porting proposal. He said he had submitted past discharge summaries and old policies with the claim and had no intention to mislead.
insurer_reason: Non-disclosure of material facts (ischaemic heart disease with CABG, paralysis, diabetes, hypertension) while porting; claim repudiated under Condition 9 and the insured's cover deleted under Condition 14.
reasoning: Although the complainant had failed to disclose his health history while porting, the Forum held that under portability rules the new insurer must itself verify medical and claim history from the previous insurer when previous policy details are furnished. Having accepted the proposal and premium without doing so, it could not use non-disclosure to wipe out long-standing continuous cover, particularly as it had not shown that the present ailment was related to the undisclosed conditions. The insurer was directed to reinstate the cover and pay the admissible claim less non-medical expenses.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Star Comprehensive policy Condition 9 (non-disclosure) and Condition 14 (cancellation)
Portability norms - verification of previous insurer's records
key_quote: it is equally the responsibility of the Insurer to verify the medical as well as claims history of the persons to be insured, from the previous insurer while accepting the proposal

case_ref: Revision Petition No. 563 of 2022 (against State Commission Chandigarh FA No. 49/2021) - Care Health Insurance Ltd. v. Harjinder Singh Sohal
insurer_name: Care Health Insurance Ltd. (formerly Religare Health Insurance)
policy_type: International / overseas travel medical insurance policy (Sept 2018 - Mar 2019)
facts: The complainant, aged over 60, bought an overseas medical insurance policy for September 2018 to March 2019 and, while in Australia, underwent coronary stenting in September and again in November 2018. Cashless and later reimbursement of about AUD 31,499 were refused for non-disclosure of coronary artery disease and dyslipidaemia, based on a 2014 hospital OPD card. In the proposal he had answered 'yes' to having a pre-existing disease and disclosed high blood pressure for 5 years, but had not ticked any of the specific listed diseases. The District Commission dismissed the complaint; the State Commission allowed it.
insurer_reason: Suppression of pre-existing coronary artery disease and dyslipidaemia in breach of utmost good faith (Clause 7.1 - disclosure of information norm); the proposer was responsible for filling all proposal form columns correctly.
reasoning: The NCDRC noted that this was not a case of a false 'no' - the complainant declared that he had a pre-existing disease and disclosed hypertension - and the insurer should have asked him to complete the blank columns or arranged a medical examination for a 60+ proposer before issuing the policy. Following Manmohan Nanda v. United India Assurance (SC), an insurer that accepts premium and issues a policy despite blank columns cannot later repudiate for non-disclosure; the insurer also had no evidence of CAD treatment beyond a single 2014 visit. The State Commission's award of the claim with interest, Rs 50,000 compensation and Rs 25,000 costs was upheld.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Manmohan Nanda v. United India Assurance Co. Ltd. (2022) 4 SCC 582, paras 55.4-55.6
Satwant Kaur Sandhu v. New India Assurance (2009) 8 SCC 316 (relied on by insurer)
Policy Clause 7.1 - disclosure of information norm
key_quote: By accepting the premium and issuing the policy despite the blank columns, the OPs cannot later repudiate the claim based on alleged suppression or non-disclosure by the complainant.
notes: amount_claimed_inr is the complainant's approximate INR equivalent of AUD 31,499 as recorded in the order.

insurer_name: Cigna TTK Health Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Cigna TTK Pro Health Insurance (sum insured Rs 10 lakh), ported from another standalone health insurer
facts: The complainant and her husband had a health policy with another insurer from 2015 and ported to the respondent in 2017, declaring the husband's diabetes. In the fourth policy year the husband was hospitalised several times - including angioplasty and then treatment for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia - and died in August 2018. The hospitalisation claim of Rs 2,17,724 was rejected because hypertension since 2013 had not been disclosed. At the hearing the complainant accepted that hypertension pre-dated the first policy and said the agent had advised them not to declare it.
insurer_reason: Non-disclosure of hypertension since 2013 (certified by a hospital) in breach of the Duty of Disclosure clause (General Terms VIII), with the admission said to be related to the pre-existing illness.
reasoning: Given that hypertension was admittedly undisclosed but the claim was for cancer treatment, the Forum asked the insurer to settle the claim excluding hypertension-related expenses. The insurer computed Rs 77,825, and the Forum awarded that amount, with interest at bank rate plus 2% if not yet paid.
rules_or_clauses_cited: General Terms and Conditions VIII - Duty of Disclosure
Portability of health insurance
key_quote: RI was asked to consider the claim for CA by excluding HTN related expenses, it being as an undisclosed ailment.

insurer_name: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Star Comprehensive Insurance Policy (sum insured Rs 5,00,000)
facts: The complainant took the policy from 30 September 2019 and renewed it. In December 2020, in the second policy year, he was admitted to ICU for cortical venous thrombosis. Cashless and reimbursement of Rs 1,15,284 were refused and he was deleted from cover because he had been hospitalised in August 2018 for deep vein thrombosis of the right leg, which was not disclosed in the proposal. He said he had recovered fully with fitness certificates, the present illness was different, and he had disclosed everything to the agent.
insurer_reason: Non-disclosure of DVT diagnosed and treated about a year before inception; the proposal answered 'no' to other diseases; claim repudiated under the non-disclosure condition and cover cancelled under Condition 12.
reasoning: The Forum relied on the 2018 DVT discharge summary and IRDAI's definition of a pre-existing disease as one diagnosed or treated within 48 months before the policy. The ailment fell within that window and the complainant produced no evidence of disclosure to the agent, so the repudiation was held to be in accordance with the policy terms and no relief was granted.
rules_or_clauses_cited: IRDAI definition of Pre-Existing Disease (48 months before policy)
Star Comprehensive policy conditions 9 and 12 - non-disclosure and cancellation
key_quote: the ailment suffered by the insured falls within 48 months prior to the effective date of the policy

forum: Supreme Court of India (civil appeal from NCDRC)
case_ref: Civil Appeal No. 2776 of 2002 - Satwant Kaur Sandhu v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd., (2009) 8 SCC 316
insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India mediclaim policy (May 1990 - May 1991)
facts: The complainant's husband took a mediclaim policy in May 1990, answering 'sound health' and 'nil' to questions on health and treatment in the proposal. He fell ill in September 1990 and died in December 1990 at a nephrology hospital. The claim of Rs 23,217.80 was repudiated after the hospital certified he was a known diabetic for 16 years with chronic renal failure on regular haemodialysis. The District Forum allowed the complaint, but the State Commission and NCDRC ruled for the insurer.
insurer_reason: Suppression of material facts about long-standing diabetes and chronic renal failure in the proposal form.
reasoning: The Supreme Court held that when a proposal form asks specific questions, the proposer must truthfully disclose facts within his knowledge, and any fact that would influence a prudent insurer's decision is material. A person on regular haemodialysis could not have been unaware of his condition, so the 'sound health' answer was untrue to his knowledge and the insurer was justified in repudiating; the appeal was dismissed.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Duty of disclosure - contract of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei)
Section 45 Insurance Act, 1938 (held not attracted)
key_quote: There was clear suppression of material facts in regard to the health of the insured and, therefore, the respondent - insurer was fully justified in repudiating the insurance contract.

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Floater Mediclaim Policy (sum insured Rs 3,00,000, enhanced from Rs 1,00,000 in 2018-19)
facts: The complainant, aged 64 and insured with the insurer since 2003, had enhanced his sum insured from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 3 lakh in 2018-19. In March 2020 he was hospitalised in Mumbai for abdominal wall cellulitis, myositis and right basal pneumonia, with newly detected uncontrolled diabetes. Against a bill of Rs 95,445 only Rs 30,289 was approved cashless, and reimbursement of the balance was denied.
insurer_reason: Diabetes is a risk factor for cellulitis and diabetes/hypertension carry a 2-year waiting period that applies to the enhanced sum insured, so the claim was assessed on the earlier Rs 1 lakh sum insured, with room rent capped at 1% of that and proportionate deduction of other charges.
reasoning: The Forum held that diabetes is not the only cause of cellulitis, which can follow any break in the skin, and that the treatment also covered myositis and pneumonia unrelated to diabetes. Applying the enhanced-sum-insured waiting period for diabetes was therefore not justified, and the insurer was directed to recompute the claim on the full Rs 3,00,000 sum insured (less non-medicals) and pay the balance.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Two-year waiting period for diabetes and hypertension applied to enhanced sum insured
Room rent 1% of sum insured with proportionate deduction
key_quote: Diabetes is not the only risk factor for Cellulitis
source_pages: PDF pages 543-548 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

insurer_name: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Family Health Optima Insurance Plan (sum insured Rs 5,00,000)
facts: The complainant's wife was covered from 17 November 2016; the policy expiring on 16 November 2017 was renewed 118 days late, from 15 March 2018. In February 2019 she underwent L5-S1 laminectomy with fixation and bone grafting in Pune. The claim of Rs 1,25,283 was rejected as falling within the 24-month waiting period for prolapse of intervertebral disc.
insurer_reason: Claim arose in the second year of cover; the 24-month waiting period under exclusion 3(ii)(a) for prolapse of intervertebral disc (other than by accident) applies, computed by excluding the renewal gap period.
reasoning: The policy allowed a 120-day grace period for renewal with continuity of waiting-period benefits. As the renewal was within that grace period, the 24-month waiting period ran from first inception and ended on 16 November 2018, before the February 2019 surgery; the insurer was wrong to subtract the gap. The claim was payable at the insurer's own assessed liability of Rs 1,01,476, with interest if paid late.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Exclusion 3(ii)(a) - 24-month waiting period for prolapse of intervertebral disc
Renewal clause - 120-day grace period with continuity of benefits
key_quote: The clause implies that there will be continuity cover if renewed within grace period.

forum: State Commission Delhi (Delhi State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission)
case_ref: First Appeal No. 579/2023 - S.B.I. General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Surojit Pachal & Anr.
insurer_name: SBI General Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: SBI General mediclaim policy from July 2017 (described as a Rs 10 lakh top-up with Rs 3 lakh general cover)
facts: The complainant took a mediclaim policy in July 2017 covering himself and his wife, who was also covered under a separate policy with another insurer. Between January and March 2018 she was hospitalised three times in Delhi for chronic renal failure and related conditions, and she died in hospital in March 2018. The other insurer paid part of the bills, but the respondent rejected reimbursement of the balance (Rs 4,66,005) and later also alleged concealment of pre-existing disease. The District Commission allowed the complaint in July 2023 and the insurer appealed.
insurer_reason: Expenses related to chronic renal failure, hypertension and diabetes and their complications are excluded for the first year of cover; alleged concealment of pre-existing disease in the proposal form.
reasoning: The insurer never produced the proposal form, the policy terms or any pre-policy medical examination, and could not show that the terms and exclusions had been supplied to the insured; concealment was not proved. Relying on Manmohan Nanda v. United India Assurance and Bharat Watch Company v. National Insurance, the Commission held that an exclusion or waiting-period clause cannot be enforced if it was never communicated. The appeal was dismissed and the District Commission's award (Rs 4,66,005 with 6% interest, Rs 30,000 compensation, Rs 10,000 costs) stood.
rules_or_clauses_cited: First-year exclusion for chronic renal failure, hypertension and diabetes (as pleaded by insurer)
Manmohan Nanda v. United India Assurance (Civil Appeal No. 8386/2013, 06.12.2021)
Bharat Watch Company v. National Insurance Co. Ltd. (Civil Appeal No. 3912/2019)
IRDA (Protection of Policyholders' Interests) Regulations, 2002
key_quote: the exclusion clause of the policy can only be resorted to if the insured has been duly supplied with the terms and conditions

insurer_name: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Medi Classic Insurance Policy (Individual), sum insured Rs 3,00,000
facts: The complainant took a fresh individual policy starting 22 May 2020. She was admitted to a Ludhiana hospital on 24 June 2020 with fever and viral pneumonia, tested positive for Covid-19 and was discharged on 7 July 2020. Cashless was refused and the reimbursement claim (Rs 2,22,249 sought) was repudiated because the doctor's pre-authorisation form recorded shortness of breath for 4 days before admission, placing the onset within the first 30 days of the policy.
insurer_reason: 30-day initial waiting period (Excl. 03): expenses for treatment of any illness within 30 days of first policy commencement are excluded (except accidents), and the insured was symptomatic within that period.
reasoning: The Ombudsman held that the illness was contracted within the first 30 days of a fresh policy, as shown by the treating doctor's pre-authorisation form noting symptoms for four days before admission. The waiting-period exclusion therefore applied and there was no deficiency on the insurer's part.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Excl. 03 - 30-day initial waiting period (not applicable to accidents or after 12 months of continuous cover)
key_quote: The admission is due to illness and same falls under the waiting period.
source_pages: PDF pages 140-142 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

insurer_name: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Family Health Optima Insurance Plan (sum insured Rs 3,00,000)
facts: The complainant's wife was covered from February 2017. About 19 months after inception, in September 2018, she was admitted to a Mumbai public hospital and underwent arthroscopic repair of a right supraspinatus (rotator cuff) tear after six months of shoulder pain. The claim (Rs 77,330) was rejected under the 24-month waiting period.
insurer_reason: 24-month waiting period for all treatment of diseases of tendons, ligaments, fascia, bones and joints other than those caused by accident (waiting period 3(ii)(d)); the medical records showed no history of trauma.
reasoning: The Forum found no record of any injury or fall - the pre-operative notes showed six months of pain - and noted that rotator cuff changes are commonly degenerative. Since an accidental cause was not established, the 24-month waiting period applied to a policy that had run only about 19 months, and the rejection was upheld.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Waiting period 3(ii)(d) - 24 months for diseases of tendon, ligament, fascia, bones and joints (other than by accident)
key_quote: In view of the fact of accidental injury not getting established, the ailment attracts 24 months waiting period.
source_pages: PDF pages 713-716 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

insurer_name: The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Oriental Insurance mediclaim policy (plan not stated in award)
facts: The complainant, insured for three consecutive years, developed sudden pain in the left eye in August 2020 and was diagnosed with central retinal vein occlusion. He was admitted to an Amritsar eye hospital on 25 August 2020 and discharged on 26 August 2020 after an intravitreal Accentrix injection, a stay of more than 24 hours. The claim of Rs 32,750 was rejected.
insurer_reason: No treatment was given on the day of admission, 24-hour hospitalisation was not needed and the patient could have been treated on OPD basis; CRVO with Accentrix injection is not in the day-care list, and the TPA treats such anti-VEGF injections as OPD procedures.
reasoning: The Ombudsman noted that the injection is given in an operation theatre under strict sterile conditions and needs post-procedure observation, and that because of technological advances most eye procedures no longer need long hospitalisation, with even minor eye incisions covered as day care. Treating the injection as eye surgery, the rejection was held improper and the admissible claim was ordered to be paid.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Policy definition of hospitalisation (minimum 24 hours)
Day-care procedures list (Appendix I)
key_quote: in my view the case is covered under eye surgery and hence payable

insurer_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Family Medicare Policy 2014 (sum insured Rs 2,00,000)
facts: The complainant, covered since 2009, was diagnosed with tuberculosis (MDR TB per the insurer) and, owing to the Covid pandemic, was treated at home on his doctor's advice. His first claim since inception, for Rs 93,490 of medical expenses, was rejected.
insurer_reason: Treatment was on OPD basis; clause 1.2.1 covers hospitalisation of at least 24 hours or specified day-care treatment, and procedures usually done on an outpatient basis are not payable.
reasoning: The Forum found there was no hospitalisation at all, the expenses related to outpatient/home treatment, and TB treatment is not a listed day-care procedure. As OPD treatment is outside the policy's cover, the repudiation was upheld despite sympathy for the complainant.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Clause 1.2.1 - minimum 24-hour hospitalisation; outpatient procedures not payable
key_quote: Since OPD treatment is not covered under the Policy, the Company's decision of repudiation of the claim is as per the terms and conditions of the policy.
source_pages: PDF pages 579-582 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Mediclaim Policy (sum insured Rs 8,00,000)
facts: The complainant, a breast cancer patient insured for about 23 years, was admitted to a Mumbai hospital on a day-care basis in December 2019, first for an intravenous zoledronic acid injection and ten days later for removal of her chemotherapy port in the operation theatre under local anaesthesia. Both claims, totalling Rs 49,225, were rejected.
insurer_reason: Hospitalisation was less than 24 hours and neither procedure is listed in the policy's day-care list (clauses 1 and 2.16); treatment could be done on OPD basis.
reasoning: The Forum treated the injection-based cancer therapy as an advancement of medical technology and noted that IRDAI's guidelines on standardisation of exclusions bar exclusion of such modern treatments; though those applied to policies from 01.10.2020, the treatment was not specifically excluded in this policy. Port removal, certified by the oncologist as requiring an OT under strict asepsis, was a day-care and not an OPD procedure. Both claims were ordered to be settled for Rs 49,225 less non-medical expenses, if any.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Policy clauses 1 and 2.16 - hospitalisation and day-care list
IRDAI Guidelines on Standardization of Exclusions in Health Insurance Contracts - modern treatment methods
key_quote: it has to be done in O.T. under strict aseptic conditions and is not an OPD procedure, the same should also be settled as a Day Care Procedure
source_pages: PDF pages 384-388 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

forum: District Commission Ernakulam (Ernakulam District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Kerala)
case_ref: CC/21/192 - Johny Milton v. Universal Sompo General Insurance Company Ltd. (as reported by LiveLaw)
insurer_name: Universal Sompo General Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Health insurance policy covering the complainant's mother (plan not stated in report)
facts: The complainant's mother, covered under his health policy, was diagnosed with myopic choroidal neovascular membrane in the left eye and received an intravitreal injection as an inpatient for day-care treatment, being discharged the same day. The reimbursement claim of Rs 27,720 was rejected. According to the report, a similar procedure undergone later that year was allowed by the insurer without objection.
insurer_reason: Treatment with the Accentrix eye injection is an outpatient procedure not requiring hospitalisation.
reasoning: The Commission held that the procedure should be viewed as day-care treatment - one that would otherwise need more than 24 hours' hospitalisation but is done in less time because of technological advancement - and that IRDAI guidelines say intravitreal injections should not be excluded. It treated the insurer's inconsistent stand on a similar later claim as an unfair trade practice and ordered reimbursement plus Rs 20,000 compensation and Rs 10,000 litigation costs.
rules_or_clauses_cited: IRDAI guidelines - intravitreal injections not to be excluded (modern treatment)
Definition of day care treatment
key_quote: This inconsistency in the Opposite Party's actions suggests an unfair trade practice
notes: Order date not given in the LiveLaw report (published 20 October 2023).

insurer_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Family Medicare Policy 2014 (sum insured Rs 10,00,000)
facts: The complainant, covered since 1997, was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma and prescribed oral chemotherapy tablets, taken without hospitalisation. Three earlier claims for the same treatment had been rejected and then allowed by the Ombudsman, but five further claims for October 2020 to March 2021, totalling Rs 1,19,079, were again rejected. He also asked that no co-payment be applied.
insurer_reason: Oral chemotherapy was taken on OPD basis, which is outside the scope of the policy under clause 1.1.
reasoning: The Forum held that modern cancer treatment such as oral chemotherapy cannot be denied, particularly when it is not specifically excluded, and cited IRDAI's Master Circular on Standardization of Health Insurance Products (22.07.2020), which requires listed modern treatments including oral chemotherapy to be covered as in-patient, domiciliary or day-care treatment. Following its earlier award for the same patient, it directed settlement of the admissible amount less non-medicals as per policy terms (including on co-payment), and held that compensation for harassment is outside its powers.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Policy clause 1.1 - scope of cover
IRDAI Master Circular on Standardization of Health Insurance Products, 22.07.2020 - modern treatment methods including oral chemotherapy
Insurance Ombudsman Rules, 2017 - no compensation for mental agony
key_quote: modern cancer treatment methods like oral chemo cannot be denied

forum: State Commission Gujarat (Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Gujarat State, Ahmedabad)
case_ref: Appeal No. 356/2023 (against District Commission Ahmedabad City (Main), Complaint No. 630/2020) - The New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Rajesh Dilsukhrai Dave
insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India mediclaim policy (sum insured Rs 5,00,000)
facts: The complainant underwent robotic nephrectomy for a large left kidney lesion at an Ahmedabad hospital in September 2019, incurring Rs 4,00,474. The insurer authorised only Rs 86,000 cashless (plus pre- and post-hospitalisation expenses) and deducted Rs 3,09,327, treating the robotic component as non-payable under the PPN package agreed between its TPA and the hospital; the complainant had paid the balance to the hospital. The District Commission ordered payment of Rs 3,09,327 with 8% interest, Rs 10,000 for mental agony and Rs 3,000 costs, and the insurer appealed.
insurer_reason: Claim limited to the PPN package rate (Rs 86,000 for nephrectomy) agreed between the TPA and the network hospital; robotic charges beyond the package not payable and the hospital charged above the agreed package.
reasoning: The State Commission held that the insurance contract is between the insured and the insurer, so a package agreement between the TPA and a hospital does not bind the insured. It noted that the IRDAI modern-treatment limit for robotic surgery quoted by the insurer applied only from 01.10.2020, after this surgery, and that under the IRDAI (TPA - Health Services) Regulations, 2016 a TPA cannot itself reject claims. The insurer's appeal was dismissed at the admission stage and the District Commission order confirmed.
rules_or_clauses_cited: IRDAI guidelines on modern treatment - robotic surgery limit (effective 01.10.2020, held inapplicable)
IRDAI (Third Party Administrators - Health Services) Regulations, 2016, Regulation 3(2)
New India Assurance v. Vikram Gohel (Punjab State Commission) - TPA cannot repudiate
key_quote: any agreement between TPA and the treating hospital are not binding either to the Insurance Company or to the insured

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Mediclaim Policy (sum insured Rs 1,00,000)
facts: The complainant's mother, insured for more than 20 years, was treated at an eye clinic for choroidal neovascular membrane of the left eye with three intravitreal anti-VEGF (Zaltrap) injections at six-week intervals between September and December 2020, each without overnight stay. Three claims totalling Rs 49,991 were rejected.
insurer_reason: Hospitalisation was less than 24 hours and the procedure is not in the day-care list (clauses 2.16 and 2.10).
reasoning: The Forum accepted that intravitreal injection is an advancement of medical technology that does not need 24 hours' hospitalisation and cited IRDAI's Master Circular of 22.07.2020, which lists intravitreal injections among modern treatments that must not be excluded. However, noting divided medical opinion on whether it is an inpatient or outpatient procedure and the repetitive nature of the treatment, it directed that the cost be shared equally and awarded 50% of the admissible expenses.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Policy clauses 2.16 (hospitalisation) and 2.10 (day care)
IRDAI Master Circular on Standardization of Health Insurance Products, 22.07.2020 - intravitreal injections
key_quote: the cost of the treatment is to be shared equally between the complainant and the Respondent

forum: State Commission Tamil Nadu (Tamil Nadu State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Chennai)
case_ref: F.A. No. 206/2019 (against CC No. 190/2016, District Commission Coimbatore) - National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Shravan Bohra
insurer_name: National Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: National Insurance mediclaim policy (November 2009 - November 2010)
facts: The complainant's wife was hospitalised repeatedly in Coimbatore between April and July 2010 and died in hospital in July 2010. After performing her last rites in his native state and staying there for several months, the complainant submitted his claim for Rs 2,80,460 in January 2011, about 9 months late. The insurer rejected it as time-barred, and rejected it again in 2015 even after the State Commission had directed it to reconsider the claim as a special case under the waiver clause.
insurer_reason: Claim not filed within 30 days of discharge as required by policy conditions 5.1, 5.3 and 5.4; delay of more than 9 months.
reasoning: Condition 5.4 itself allowed waiver of the time limit in extreme hardship, and the insurer did not dispute the treatment, the bills or the death - late submission was the only ground. Given the bereavement and the earlier direction to treat the claim as a special case, repudiation was unjustified. The Commission upheld payment of Rs 2,80,460 but reduced interest to 6% from the date of complaint and set aside compensation because the delay was admitted (costs of Rs 5,000 retained).
rules_or_clauses_cited: Policy condition 5.4 - claim within 30 days of discharge, with waiver in cases of extreme hardship
key_quote: especially when there is no denial of the claim for anyother reason except for the delayed submission

forum: State Commission Delhi (Delhi State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission)
case_ref: First Appeal No. 151/2025 - Star Health & Allied Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Om Dev
insurer_name: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Young Star Insurance Policy (floater), sum insured Rs 5,00,000
facts: The complainant bought an online floater policy in December 2021 and was hospitalised in a private Delhi hospital from 23 to 25 April 2022 for enteric fever, paying a bill of Rs 48,089. He informed the insurer on 30 April 2022, about seven days after admission. The claim was rejected; the District Commission allowed it with Rs 50,000 compensation, and the insurer appealed.
insurer_reason: Intimation was not given within 24 hours of hospitalisation (claim notification condition 2D), depriving the insurer of the chance to verify; the indoor case records were in stereotyped handwriting with tampering and discrepancies, and investigation indicated a fraudulent claim (Condition 1 - misrepresentation).
reasoning: The State Commission held that the insured deliberately delayed intimation in breach of the 24-hour notification condition, which must be strictly construed. It also relied on the investigator's report (address untraceable, a pattern of similar claims filed through the same representative, who was also an agent, and the same doctor across hospitals), found the patient's vitals normal so that hospitalisation was unwarranted, and concluded the claim was a design to defraud. The District Commission's order was set aside. Note: late intimation was combined with strong fraud findings.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Standard Condition 2D - notification of claim within 24 hours
Condition 1 - misrepresentation/non-disclosure
Industrial Promotion & Investment Corporation of Orissa v. New India Assurance - strict construction
key_quote: the Respondent cannot be allowed to seek relief for its own wrong

insurer_name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Arogya Raksha Policy (sum insured Rs 7,00,000)
facts: The complainant had left-eye cataract surgery at a Mumbai hospital in February 2020 and claimed Rs 37,800. He complied with the TPA's requirements, but the claim stayed unsettled for more than a year because the insurer insisted on a separate invoice for the intraocular lens (Rs 7,300), which the hospital had not issued.
insurer_reason: Claim kept pending for non-submission of the IOL invoice; in any case the policy limits cataract surgery to Rs 25,000.
reasoning: The hospital's final bill already showed the IOL charge along with surgeon, OT, anaesthesia and other heads, so insisting on a separate invoice and withholding the claim for over a year was unjustified. The claim was payable up to the policy's Rs 25,000 cataract limit, with interest at 2% above bank rate from one month after submission of the final documents.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Policy cap of Rs 25,000 for cataract surgery
Interest for delayed settlement (2% above bank rate)
key_quote: withholding the claim for over a year for such a small and reasonable amount is not justified

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India New Mediclaim 2012 Policy (sum insured Rs 5,00,000)
facts: The complainant, insured since 1996, had coronary angioplasty in Mumbai in September 2017. Of total claims of Rs 3,99,557 (cashless plus pre- and post-hospitalisation), Rs 40,158 remained unpaid. Deductions were made for consultation, investigation and CT scan charges for want of reports, physiotherapy bills without dates, a medicine bill without prescription, stent price above the government cap, excess room rent, dietician charges and non-medical items; the complainant said all documents had already been given to the TPA.
insurer_reason: Supporting documents not submitted (doctor's notes, 2D echo/ECG/stress test and CT scan reports, prescription); physiotherapy bills without dates and break-up; coronary stent price capped by government notification; room rent restriction; dietician and non-medical charges not payable.
reasoning: The Forum asked the complainant to resubmit the CT scan and other reports and prescriptions so those expenses could be paid, allowed the physiotherapy prescribed by the cardiologist, and held the excess stent charge must be reimbursed because the patient has no control over hospital billing (the insurer may recover any overcharge from the hospital). Deductions for excess room rent, dietician charges and non-medical items were upheld, and Rs 34,577 was awarded.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Claim documentation requirements (reports, prescriptions)
Government price cap on coronary stents
Room rent restriction and non-medical items
key_quote: the patient has no control on the same and has genuinely paid the amount as billed by the hospital

insurer_name: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: New India Floater Mediclaim Policy (2018-19)
facts: The complainant's 21-year-old daughter, covered under the family floater policy (family insured since 2002), was admitted for 12 days in April-May 2019 for a lumbar slipped disc with sciatica that worsened after gym exercise. Treatment consisted of acupuncture, physiotherapy, massage, TENS, ultrasound and posture correction. The claim of Rs 1,39,185 was repudiated; the family said a similar claim at the same hospital had been paid in 2012, which the insurer disputed.
insurer_reason: Acupuncture and physiotherapy treatment is excluded under exclusion clause 4.4.18.
reasoning: The Forum found that the hospital treatment was essentially acupuncture and physiotherapy with virtually no other medical management, both of which are specifically excluded by clause 4.4.18. The repudiation was therefore in accordance with the policy and no relief was granted.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Exclusion clause 4.4.18 - acupuncture and physiotherapy
key_quote: Exclusion Clause 4.4.18 specifically excludes Acupuncture & Physiotherapy treatment
source_pages: PDF pages 328-331 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation

insurer_name: Star Health and Allied Insurance Co. Ltd.
policy_type: Star Comprehensive Insurance Policy (sum insured Rs 7,50,000)
facts: The complainant, covered with the insurer since 2015, underwent laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (bariatric surgery) for obesity with BMI 43, sleep apnoea and osteoarthritis at a non-network Pune hospital in September 2020. She had intimated the claim within 24 hours of admission, and her agent had been told by customer care that bariatric surgery was claimable up to Rs 2,50,000; no one told her it had to be done cashless at a network hospital. The reimbursement claim of Rs 3,84,774 was rejected.
insurer_reason: Obesity is not covered under the main hospitalisation section; bariatric surgery is payable only under Section 6 as an additional benefit up to Rs 2,50,000, on a cashless basis with prior approval, subject to special conditions (36-month waiting period, BMI criteria, opinion of two surgeons).
reasoning: The Forum held that it cannot go beyond the regulator-approved policy terms, under which bariatric surgery is payable only on a cashless basis with prior approval, so the reimbursement claim failed. It nevertheless recorded that the agent and insurer had not guided the policyholder about this condition and directed the insurer to prevent such lapses.
rules_or_clauses_cited: Star Comprehensive policy Section 6 - bariatric surgery benefit (cashless only, prior approval, special conditions)
key_quote: the complainant was not provided timely guidance in respect of the policy conditions by the Agent and the Company officials as well
source_pages: PDF pages 482-486 of the April 2021 health-insurance award compilation
